Hi,

I really appreciate your help.
But I'm having a hard time wrapping my head around these concepts.

Let me try and simplify the problem. Let's say I have single input file like this:

row1
row2
...
row200000

and I just want to produce output like this:

key: row1
value: <some random number>
key: row2
value: <some random number>
...
key: row200000
value: <some random number>

There is only one step to the computation (so there's a map step but no reducer, or vice versa if that is an option), and let's say that the computation on each row takes a significant amount of time, and we're concerned with speed, so we want to make this as parallel as possible.
For our purposes, the random number can be generated with runif(1).

What would be the Rhipe code that would do this?

If instead the user had an R session on a cluster with 1000 cores, they could compute 1000 rows as quickly as they could solve for one on their laptop.  MPI becomes fragile and unreliable with a cluster of this size, but Rhipe intrigues me because Hadoop is designed to be robust to nodes failing, etc.
I want to hide all the Rhipe/Hadoop details from the user, and just take a function that the user defines, which can compute a single row.
So, being able to solve a silly problem like the one posed above is important to my understanding of how to make such a framework.

Thanks much,
Dan

> Saptarshi

simulator <- function(inputfile,Numsplits){
  list(mapreduce.input.lineinputformat.linespermap=Numsplits,
       parse.ifolder=FALSE,
       rhipe_input_folder=inputfile,
       rhipe_inputformat_class="org.godhuli.rhipe.RNLineInputFormat",
       rhipe_inputformat_keyclass="org.godhuli.rhipe.RHNumeric",
       rhipe_inputformat_valueclass="org.godhuli.rhipe.RHText")
}

m <- rhmap({
  'r' is a string corresponding to a row
  rhcollect(k, F(r))
})

results <- rhwatch(rhmr(map=m,mapred=simulator("/user/sguha/tmp/testfile",5),param=list(F=F)))

Here testfile has 24 rows, simulator creates a job with 5 parallel splits each of ~4 elements each.
F is a user defined function.

Note: when you have 200K splits and you want to read all quickly from the HDFS (remember we're reading 200K key-value pairs)
there are smater ways to read.

[1] https://github.com/downloads/saptarshiguha/RHIPE/Rhipe_0.69.tar.gz

## kill jobs.
## here mon.sec=Inf - it just waits (and prints to output)
first.step <- rhwatch(rhmr(map=rhmap({ rhcollect(k, runif(100)) }),reduce=0,N=1000),read=FALSE,mon.sec=Inf)

if(first.step[[1]]$state !="SUCCEEDED" || first.step[[1]]$rerrors == TRUE)
  stop("Job 1 Did not Complte")

## Note how first.step is ifolder! Since no output folder was given in above
## RHIPE creates a folder in rhoptions()$HADOOP.TMP (you should set it)
## and if read=FALSE in the above call, first.step contains infor about this output folder
## you can clean the tmp folder of all these temp files with a call to 'rhclean'

next.step <-  rhwatch(rhmr(map..., ifolder=first.step),read=FALSE)

## read the results back in
final.result <- rhread(next.step)

a great combination for doing analytics on terabytes of data.

Jim
